title: Carmel at fifteen (1888)
hookLine: she gets the door she begged for at fifteen, and finds the cross waiting just inside
tomorrow: a little girl sees a man with his face covered. who was he?

cards: New jobs come with a welcome packet: the smiling photo, the free hoodie, the promise that you'll love it here. The first real week usually looks different. Thérèse has fought for this door.
She asked a pope for it. Now it's morning in Lisieux, and she kneels outside the enclosure of the Carmelite convent to ask her father's blessing. He kneels too, and blesses her through his tears.
The door opens. She's fifteen, and she walks in. Everything she begged for is on the other side.
So what does she find there?

teach.b: Not roses. In The Story of a Soul she says the life was just what she had pictured, and no sacrifice took her by surprise. She hadn't come for a dream, so there was no dream to lose.
And still, she writes, suffering held out its arms to her from her first steps, and she threw herself into them with love. Not at the end of a long road. In the first days.
What did that look like? Small, hard things. Prayer often felt dry; she calls that dryness her daily bread.
Her prioress was strict with her; Thérèse says she could hardly cross her path without being corrected.

teach.h: A COBWEB, A CHILD OF FIFTEEN.
teach.b: She tells, with some humor, of a cobweb she missed in the cloister, and the prioress remarking that anyone could see it had been swept by a child of fifteen. So why stay?

teach.h: TO SAVE SOULS, TO PRAY FOR PRIESTS.
teach.b: At her examination before her vows, she says, she gave her reason plainly: she had come to save souls, and above all to pray for priests. A reason that size can carry a cobweb.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the saint people picture holding roses says suffering met her at the door.
The cross came first, and she didn't take it as a sign she'd chosen wrong. She took it as part of the road in.

how: Carmelite nuns live an enclosed life of prayer, work and silence, and Catholics remember Thérèse as entering young and accepting its hardships from her first days there.

games.q: your cousin got into the nursing program she dreamed about. week one: a strict instructor, a night shift, tears in the parking lot. she asks if it's a sign to quit. what do Thérèse's first days say?
o: a hard start isn't a verdict; hold on to the reason you came.
if it were right for her, it would feel right from day one.
she should hide how hard it is and act like she loves it.
games.why: Thérèse got the life she begged for and found suffering at the door. She didn't read it as a mistake; her reason, souls and priests, carried the hard days.

practice: Find a scrap of paper and write one line about a beginning that's hard for you right now: a new job, a new school, a new diagnosis, a new grief. Under it, write the reason you're still there.
Then let the paper rest in your lap while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: Carmel at fifteen. A girl who got exactly what she asked for, and found the cross waiting just inside the door.

orig.note: Latin for cross: the word behind her line that suffering met her at the very start.

carryVoice: Your line: the cross first. A hard start isn't the same as a wrong turn. See you tomorrow.
